title: Code Wheel
context: Grade 4. An adult sees a puzzle. What is actually being learnt is that a code is one pattern applied to every letter, that the key is the rule, and that decoding is the same rule run backwards. The page's summary box says that to decode a secret code we must know the key, and the locked mode makes that true in the child's hands rather than on the page: without the key, several readings stand on the strip at once and nothing chooses between them.

writeup.why: Set a key, write a word in code with it, and read a code back by undoing the key, then find out why the key is needed at all.
writeup.look: Two rings of letters one inside the other, a number band that clips round them, and a message strip along the foot of the stage.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only. 'Code Wheel' sits in ink at the far left, with a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it. The phase title sits beside the dot on the same line, then the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart stand as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the letters carried against the letters in this phase's message, two numbers in ink. The first climbs by one as each letter drops into the strip or each trial row is written out, and the second is fixed at the length of the message. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The wheel sits at the left of the working area. The number band, when clipped on, is a ring 400 across at 64,212. Inside it the outer ring of letters is 340 across and the inner ring 250 across, all three sharing one centre at 264,412. Each ring carries the twenty-six letters evenly spaced, so Z sits beside A with no end anywhere. The place where Z meets A carries a small reddish purple tick on every ring. The outer ring is fixed. The inner ring turns one letter place per step, and the places turned are written on the key tag, 200 by 60 at 600,222. The number band writes each letter's place beside it, one to twenty-six, and flips to run from twenty-six down to one. A small arrow on the band shows which way it runs and what A is. The swap key draws chords straight across the ring from each letter to its partner: the first to the last, the second to the second last. The message strip runs along the foot of the working area, 1080 by 96 at 64,628, with a plain letter box above a code box for each letter. Tapping a letter on the outer ring draws a vermilion line from it to its partner under the current key, one place at a time. The partner then drops into the strip under the plain letter. Undo turns the wheel back by the key and carries each code letter back along the same kind of line. The trial rows stand at the right, 540 by 316 at 600,296, one row to a trial. In the locked mode each key tried is written at the left of its row with its reading in full beside it, and no row is marked until the key is shown. Down the right of the canvas the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92), which holds what the child has given. That rectangle is the same on every phase and is never animated in or out. Under it is the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twenty-six letter keys, seven across in four rows with the last row holding five. Twelve number keys three across take over wherever a code is written in numbers. On the fourth phase two more keys stand under them, sure and cannot be sure. The footer runs 758 to 900. The voice caption sits at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling. The phase bar sits at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, taken from its pictures. Whatever the stage hands over is deep blue: a given term, a bead, the bottom row of a tower, a plain letter, a tile already laid. The first member of a repeating group is deep blue too, and the second member, or a second kind set beside the first, is amber. The step itself is vermilion in every tool without exception: a jump arc and its label, a quarter turn, an operation sign, a key's shift. Whatever the rule makes is green: a next term, a built box, a coded or decoded letter, a copy just laid, a tick. Whatever the child is asked to notice is reddish purple: a broken box, a closed-in gap, a doubled part, a leftover counter, a line put back. The dots of dotted paper are grey and nothing else is. Every bracket, outline, rule and blank is near-black chrome. Chrome never borrows a content colour, and no content colour is ever used for chrome. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a thing is told by its label or its place before it is told by its colour. A blank waiting for the child is an empty outlined box, never a faded copy of its answer. The alphabet is never drawn as a straight line on this stage, not even in a heading. A line has two ends, and an end is exactly where a letter falls off when a key moves it on.
writeup.finish: The card shows the wheel set to the last key the child used, the message strip with a word in code and in plain letters, and the trial rows from the locked message.

phases.win: the numbers drop into the strip, one under each letter
phases.does: taps each letter of a word and reads its number off the band into the strip
phases.goal: a key says what every letter stands for, such as A as one up to Z as twenty-six
phases.says: Find each letter on the ring. What number does the key give it?
phases.check: Away from the screen: write your name with A as one. Then ask a friend to read it back.
phases.feels: every letter has one partner under the key, and the same letter always gets the same one
phases.hands: Write the alphabet round the edge of a paper plate and number each letter from one, starting at A. Have each child write their own name in code with it and pass it to a partner to read back. Then number the plate the other way, with A as twenty-six, and ask what the same name becomes. Ask what the partner needed to know before they could read it.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: what number does the band give A? Second rung, the phase's: which way is the band running? Third rung: the word is cut to its first letter, and the child counts round the band from A to it. The letter keys and the number keys stay open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: counting on a ruler starts from zero, and the first mark on anything measured has always been the nought.
wrong.move: counts the alphabet from zero, so every number comes out one too small and KITE is written ten, eight, nineteen, four.
wrong.screen: the band counts from A again, lighting each letter as it is counted and writing one under A. The child's numbers stay in the strip, and the band's numbers are written above them, each one bigger. Nothing is cleared.

wrong.why: the first key met ran from A as one, and a band of numbers looks the same whichever way it runs.
wrong.move: reads the numbers off the band as if it ran from A as one, when it has been flipped to run from A as twenty-six.
wrong.screen: the small arrow on the band lights, with A's own number written beside it. The child's line stays in the strip, and the flipped band's number for each letter is carried down beside it, so S, U and N read eight, six and thirteen.

phases.screen: the outer ring with the number band clipped round it and an empty message strip
phases.soWhat: A key says what every letter stands for, such as A as one up to Z as twenty-six.
phases.concept: A key says what each letter stands for

phases.win: the coded word fills the strip, and a letter near the end is carried round to the start
phases.does: carries each letter of the word to its partner on the inner ring
phases.goal: a key can move every letter the same number of places on, and Z comes round to A
phases.says: Move each letter the same number of places. What comes after the last letter?
phases.check: Move every letter of ZIP three places on, and say what happened to the Z.
phases.feels: every letter moves the same number of places, and the ring carries Z on round to A
phases.hands: Pin two paper circles together at the centre, each with the alphabet round its edge, and turn the inner one three letters on. Carry a short word across letter by letter, touching each landing. Then carry a word with Y or Z in it and ask what comes after Z. Let the circle answer: there is no end to fall off.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many places does the key move each letter? Second rung, the phase's: what comes after Z on the ring? Third rung: the word is cut to one letter near the end of the alphabet, and the child carries it one place at a time. The letter keys stay open.

wrong.why: every written alphabet the class has seen ends at Z, and a line that ends has nothing past its end.
wrong.move: stops at Z because nothing comes after it, and leaves that letter out of the code.
wrong.screen: the carry line from Z runs on round the ring one place at a time, past the tick where Z meets A, lighting A, then B, then C. Each landing is numbered as it lights. The child's code keeps its empty box, and the ring's landing is written beside it.

wrong.why: a jump is easy to count by the letters touched, and the first letter touched is the one the finger is already on.
wrong.move: counts the letter it starts on as the first place, so three places on from O lands on Q instead of R.
wrong.screen: the carry runs one place at a time from O, and the first number is written on P, the first landing. O itself is left unnumbered. The child's Q stays in the strip, and the count stops on R with three written over it.

phases.screen: both rings, the inner ring turned a few places on, and a word waiting
phases.soWhat: A key can move every letter the same number of places on, and moving on past Z carries on round from A.

phases.win: the message reads out in plain letters, and a letter that passed A comes round from Z
phases.does: turns the inner ring back by the key and reads each letter's partner
phases.goal: decoding moves each letter back as far as the key moved it on
phases.says: The key moved each letter on. Which way do you go to undo it?
phases.check: A key moved every letter two places on. The code reads E C V. What was the word? Code it again to check.
phases.feels: the key moved each letter on, so undoing it moves each one back just as far
phases.hands: Hand a partner a coded word and tell them the key: three places on. Ask which way they must go to undo it, and let them try both ways on the paper wheel. Then have them code their answer again with the key and compare it with the message they were given. If the two match, the word is found.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which way did the key move the letters? Second rung, the phase's: which way do you go to undo it? Third rung: the message is cut to one letter, and the child turns the ring back one place at a time. The letter keys stay open.

wrong.why: the key said on, and doing what the key says feels like obeying it.
wrong.move: moves each letter three places on again instead of back, reading F D N H as I G Q K.
wrong.screen: the child's reading is coded again through the key and set under the message. It comes out L J T N, further from the code rather than back to it. Undo then turns the wheel back three places and carries each code letter home. Both readings stay in the strip.

wrong.why: going back feels like counting down, and a count down stops at the start.
wrong.move: going back past A, stops at A, so D F P never becomes a word.
wrong.screen: the carry line runs back from D one place at a time, past the tick where A meets Z, lighting C, B, A, Z and then Y. Each landing is numbered as it lights. The child's box keeps what was written, and the ring's landing is written beside it.

phases.screen: a coded message in the strip with its key written beside it
phases.soWhat: Decoding moves each letter back as far as the key moved it on, and going back past A carries on round from Z.

phases.win: several readings stand in the trial rows, and the right one lights only when the key is shown
phases.does: tries one key after another, writes each reading out, and says what would settle it
phases.goal: without the key the same code can be read in more than one way
phases.says: Try a key. Now try another. Which one did the sender use?
phases.check: Away from the screen: send a friend a code with no key. How many readings can they find before you tell them?
phases.feels: several readings stand side by side, and nothing on the strip says which one the sender meant
phases.hands: Write three, one, two on the board with no key, and ask the class what it says. Collect every reading they can make, with A as one, with A as twenty-six, or with a key that moves letters along. Write each one out in full in a column. Then show the key, and ask what the key did that none of the readings could do.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which key did you try? Second rung, the phase's: could another key read it too? Third rung: the message is cut to one number, and the child reads it under two keys. The trial rows stay open.

wrong.why: a reading that makes a real word feels like proof, and the first key met is the one the hand reaches for.
wrong.move: reads the code with A as one, finds a word, and takes it as certain.
wrong.screen: the trial rows keep the child's reading and add the others, each written out in full with its key at the left of its row. Four, fifteen, seven reads D O G in one row and W L T in the next. No row is marked, and the key tag stays closed until the key is shown.

wrong.why: that key came first, and a code with no key named looks as though it must use the one already known.
wrong.move: tries only the key with A as one, and gives up when it does not make a word.
wrong.screen: the locked mode sets out the other keys the chapter uses, the flipped band, a key that moves letters along, and the swap. It writes a trial row for each in turn. The child's single row stays at the top.

phases.screen: a coded message with its key hidden and the trial rows empty
phases.soWhat: Without the key the same code can be read in more than one way, so to decode a secret code you must know the key.
phases.concept: Without the key the code stays locked

writeup.delight: The third phase, once the message reads out in plain letters. The plain word lifts off the strip and rides forward round the wheel through the key, letter by letter, and each letter lands exactly on the code box it came from. The two lines of the strip then stand one above the other, joined letter to letter by short vermilion ticks. It runs as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the outer ring stands with the number band clipped round it and a word waiting above an empty message strip. On the second both rings stand with the inner ring already turned a few places on, the key tag showing how many, and a word waiting. On the third a coded message lies in the strip with its key written on the tag and the plain letter boxes empty. On the fourth a coded message lies in the strip with the key tag closed and the trial rows empty. The running count at the top left holds the letters carried against the letters in this phase's message, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the first letter of the word, or of the message, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks what the key does to it. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any key, a turn of the inner ring, a number band either way or the swap key, with the message strip and the locked mode open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on number keys and a swap key, keys that move letters along, decoding by undoing the key, and why the key is needed to read a code.
voiceLines: Two rings of letters, one inside the other. Turn the inner ring to set a key.
Find each letter on the ring. What number does the key give it?
Move each letter the same number of places. What comes after the last letter?
The key moved each letter on. Which way do you go to undo it?
Try a key. Now try another. Which one did the sender use?
Another word. Say the key out loud before you carry a letter.
Free play. Any key, any word, with the strip and the locked message open.
Carry the letter again, one place at a time, and count as you go.
Words written in code and read back out, and every key named.

observations.why: A key is one rule for every letter, so it gives each letter one partner.
observations.soWhat: Anyone holding the key can write the code or read it.
observations.observe: Every letter had one number under the key, and the same letter always had the same number.

observations.why: The letters sit round a circle, so the place after Z is the place where A is.
observations.soWhat: Moving on past Z carries on round from A.
observations.observe: A letter carried on past Z came round to A without anything special happening.

observations.why: Undoing the key moves each letter back exactly as far as the key moved it on.
observations.soWhat: Decoding is the key run backwards, and coding the answer again is the check.
observations.observe: Coding the decoded word again gave back the code, letter for letter.

observations.why: The same letters or numbers stand for different things under different keys.
observations.soWhat: To decode a secret code you must know the key.
observations.observe: Two keys read the same message two ways, and nothing on the strip chose between them.

serves.exercise: decoding the two messages written with a key that moves each letter two places on

source_tool.description: Two rings of letters sit one inside the other in the middle of the stage, the outer ring holding the alphabet from A to Z and the inner ring free to turn. Turned a few places, the inner ring sets a key that moves every letter the same number of places on, and because the letters sit round a circle, Z is followed by A with nothing to explain: the last letter simply comes round to the first. A number band can be clipped round the outer ring instead, giving each letter its place in the alphabet from one to twenty-six, or running the other way from twenty-six down to one. A swap key pairs the first letter with the last, the second with the second last, and so on, drawn as chords straight across the ring. A message strip along the foot of the stage takes a word a letter at a time: the child taps a letter on the outer ring, the key carries it along a drawn line to its partner, and the partner drops into the strip. To decode, the same wheel runs backwards, the inner ring turned back by as many places as the key moved on. A locked mode hands over a message with the key hidden and lets the child try keys one at a time, each trial written out in full under the last, so that more than one reading can be seen to fit.
source_tool.art_direction: Two paper rings of letters, pinned / Picture book

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a strip of picture cells, a paper arrow on a dial, stepping stones with jump arcs between them, counters that pair up, a tower of boxes each resting on two below, two rings of letters that turn, a ruled board of sums with a slate beside it, and a bench of dotted paper with a tray of tiles.
A repeating group is always shown whole. When a bracket is drawn over it, every copy of it along the row is lit at once, and a copy that does not match is left unlit rather than hidden.

Every step in a series is drawn as an arc from one term to the next with its label on the arc, never as a bare number between two terms, so the step between every pair of neighbours can be read, not only the first.
A counting-down track has a zero stone at its left end and nothing beyond it. No track, board or list is ever drawn running on past zero.

Every box of a number tower rests visibly on exactly two boxes below it, and the operation sign is drawn between each pair of neighbours in every row, so a tower that keeps to one operation shows the same sign all the way up.
The alphabet is always drawn round a circle, twenty-six letters evenly spaced, so the last letter sits beside the first and no letter ever falls off an end.
A line put back into a board is drawn sliding into its place between its neighbours, and the jump labels either side of it are rewritten where they stand, never cleared.

Tiles are drawn at true relative size, edge to edge where they touch, never overlapping unless the frame is showing an overlap on purpose, and a circle is never squeezed to close a gap. A tile drawn taller than it is wide is never called a square.
A shape, a term or a box is told apart by its label or its position first and by its colour second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a shape, a term, a box, a letter or a tile the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, taken from the pictures, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. Whatever the stage hands over, a printed term, a bead, the bottom row of a tower, a plain letter of a message and a tile already laid, is deep blue, and so is the first member of a repeating group. The second member of a repeating group, and a second kind set beside the first, is amber. The step itself, a jump arc and its label, a quarter turn, the operation sign between two boxes and the shift a key makes from a letter to its partner, is vermilion, in every tool without exception, because a chapter whose whole subject is the rule cannot afford a frame where the step has to be hunted for. Whatever the rule makes, a next term, a box built from the two below it, a coded or decoded letter, a tile carried on and a tick on the can do list, is green. Whatever the child is asked to notice, a box that breaks the tower's operation, a space with tiles closed round it, a part where two tiles lie on top of each other, a counter left without a partner and a missing line put back on a board, is reddish purple. The dots of dotted paper are grey and nothing else is. Every bracket, outline, rule and blank is near-black chrome, and the outer edge of a tiled patch is traced in that plain line and never filled, because it is where the tiling stops and not a gap. A blank waiting for the child is an empty outlined box and never a faded copy of its answer. All of that holds in greyscale, because a jump label sits on its own arc, a broken box keeps its light on after the check has moved past it, a closed-in gap is filled while the outer edge is only outlined, and a leftover counter stands apart from the pairs.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.

phase_map.concept: A key says what each letter stands for
Without the key the code stays locked

placement.where: After two paper circles have been pinned together and turned by hand to make a class code, and before the printed messages are decoded. The tool is what keeps the alphabet round a circle, so the last letter is followed by the first without a rule to remember, and what writes several readings of one message side by side while its key is hidden.

answer_key.rule: A key says what each letter stands for. With A as one, each letter stands for its place in the alphabet, up to Z as twenty-six, and the numbers can run the other way, with A as twenty-six and Z as one. A key can move every letter the same number of places on; the alphabet goes round like a circle, so moving on past Z carries on round from A. Another key swaps the first letter with the last, the second with the second last, and so on. To decode, undo the key: move each letter back by as many places as the key moved it on, going round from Z when you pass A, or read each number back to its letter. Without the key a code cannot be read for certain, because the same letters or numbers stand for different things under different keys.
answer_key.wrong: The wheel is turned again one place at a time with the places counted aloud, and the letter is carried from the outer ring to its partner along a drawn line, so the child sees which way and how far it moved. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: K is the 11th letter of the alphabet, so it becomes 11.
I is the 9th letter and T is the 20th, so they become 9 and 20.
E is the 5th letter, so KITE is written 11 9 20 5.
items.question: With A as 1, B as 2 and so on up to Z as 26, write the word KITE in code.
items.checkpoint: A key tells you what every letter stands for.
items.misconception: Counting the alphabet from 0 instead of 1, so every number comes out one too small.

steps: Z is the last letter, so moving on three places goes round: A, B, C. Z becomes C.
O moves three places on: P, Q, R. So O becomes R.
The second O also becomes R, so ZOO is written C R R.
items.question: A key moves every letter three places on, so A becomes D, and X, Y and Z go round to A, B and C. Write the word ZOO in this code.
items.checkpoint: The alphabet goes round like a circle, so moving on past Z carries on from A.
items.misconception: Stopping at Z because nothing comes after it, and leaving the letter out.

steps: To decode, undo the key: move each letter three places back.
F goes back to C, D goes back to A, N goes back to K and H goes back to E.
So the word was CAKE, and moving each letter three places on again gives F D N H back.
items.question: A key moved every letter three places on. The code reads F D N H. What was the word?
items.checkpoint: Decoding means moving each letter back as far as the key moved it on.
items.misconception: Moving the letters three more places on, which hides the word further instead of finding it.

steps: With A as 1, 4 is D, 15 is O and 7 is G, which spells DOG.
With A as 26 and Z as 1, 4 is W, 15 is L and 7 is T.
The same numbers give different letters under different keys, so only the key settles what was meant.
items.answer: With A as 1 it reads DOG, and with A as 26 it reads W L T. Without the key you cannot be sure which was meant
items.question: A friend sends the code 4 15 7 with no key. Read it with A as 1, and then with A as 26 and Z as 1. Can you be sure what it says?
items.checkpoint: To decode a secret code you must know the key.
items.misconception: Taking the first reading that makes a word as certain, when another key could hide another word.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: With A as 1 and Z as 26, write the word SUN in code.
A key swaps A with Z, B with Y, C with X, and so on. Write the word FLY in this code.
A key moves every letter four places on. Write the word PEN in this code.
A key moves every letter three places on. Write the word YES in this code.
items.final_answer: B H V, because Y goes round past Z to B

items.question: A key moved every letter four places on. The code reads F S S O. What was the word?
A key moved every letter five places on. The code reads D F P. What was the word?
items.final_answer: YAK, because D goes back five places, past A and round from Z, to Y

items.question: The code K D W was made by moving every letter the same number of places on, but the key is lost. Moving back three places gives HAT. Moving back one place gives J C V. Can you be sure which is the message?
items.final_answer: Not for certain. HAT is the only reading that makes a word, but only the key can settle it, because another key could hide another word

items.question: Make a key that moves every letter six places on, and write the word ANT in it. What must a friend be told before they can read it?
items.final_answer: G T Z, and the friend must be told the key, six places on, so they can move each letter six places back

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: holds the alphabet from A to Z round a circle
turns to set how many places on the key moves each letter
gives each letter its place, one to twenty-six, or the other way round
pairs the first letter with the last, the second with the second last, and so on
takes a word a letter at a time and shows it in code
runs the wheel backwards by the key to decode
hides the key so that keys can be tried one at a time
write each trial reading out in full under the last

teaching_notes: Make the paper code wheel from the activity before the tool is opened: two circles with the alphabet round each edge, pinned at the centre. Turning the inner circle settles the one thing a written table cannot, that the letter after Z is A, because on a circle there is no end to fall off. The page shows three kinds of key: each letter as its place in the alphabet, with a note that the numbers can run the other way; each letter moved one place on; and a note swapping the first letter with the last. The printed exercise then uses a key that moves each letter two places on, so decoding it means going two places back. Use other words and other keys in class, so the printed messages are still worth decoding when the class reaches them. The page calls the numbers of a code digits, when most of them have two digits; call them numbers. Its summary box prints the sentence about the key with no spaces between the words. Write it on the board with the spaces put back and read it aloud: to decode a secret code, we must know the key. Then let the locked mode prove it.
generation_prompt: Build a code wheel tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. Two concentric rings sit in the middle of the working area, each carrying the twenty-six letters evenly spaced round it; the outer ring is fixed and the inner ring turns one letter place per step, with the number of places turned shown beside it. A number band can be clipped round the outer ring, writing each letter's place in the alphabet from one to twenty-six beside it, and flipped to run from twenty-six down to one. A swap key draws a chord across the ring from each letter to its partner, the first to the last, the second to the second last. A message strip along the foot of the working area takes a word letter by letter: the child taps a letter on the outer ring, a line is drawn to its partner under the current key, and the partner drops into the strip under the plain letter. An undo control runs the wheel backwards by the key and reads a coded message back into plain letters. A locked mode hides the key and lets the child set keys one at a time, writing each trial reading out in full in a row under the last, with nothing marked right until the key is shown. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Turn the inner ring to set the key. Tap each letter of your word. Read its partner into the strip. To decode, turn the ring back the same way. Without the key, try one key at a time.
